pr_title: Ensure Enumerable methods are preserved by System.Linq.Querable
pr_body:
When using System.Linq.Queryable against an in-memory collection, and trimming the application, the underlying Enumerable methods need to be preserved by the linker.

Annotating each Queryable method with a DynamicDependency to the corresponding Enumerable method will fix this scenario.

Fix #42536

cc @marek-safar @pranavkm

I think it goes down to https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/c48127daec460692ee18f7ae7552bcc3f7fa8499/src/libraries/System.Linq.Queryable/src/System/Linq/EnumerableRewriter.cs#L218 which is recognized by linker as unfriendly and issues warning which is ignored by libraries build.

For a 5.0 app, you can turn off trimming by configuring `<PublishTrimmed>false</PublishTrimmed>` in your project file.
@ElderJames - do you have a branch of the repo that is targeting `net5.0`?

> Thanks @lewing ,
> 
> I tried, but it was still the exception.

Whoops, I gave the wrong instructions, try https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/42536#issuecomment-696802055 instead

I can repro this error with this simple change to the `FetchData` page of a `dotnet new blazorwasm` template app:

```diff
    protected override async Task OnInitializedAsync()
    {
        forecasts = await Http.GetFromJsonAsync<WeatherForecast[]>("sample-data/weather.json");

+        forecasts = forecasts.AsQueryable().Take(2).ToArray();
    }
```

```
blazor.webassembly.js:1 crit: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Rendering.WebAssemblyRenderer[100]
      Unhandled exception rendering component: Arg_NullReferenceException
System.NullReferenceException: Arg_NullReferenceException
   at System.Linq.EnumerableRewriter.FindEnumerableMethod(String name, ReadOnlyCollection`1 args, Type[] typeArgs)
   at System.Linq.EnumerableRewriter.VisitMethodCall(MethodCallExpression m)
   at System.Linq.Expressions.MethodCallExpression.Accept(ExpressionVisitor visitor)
   at System.Linq.Expressions.ExpressionVisitor.Visit(Expression node)
   at System.Linq.EnumerableQuery`1[[BlazorApp3.Pages.FetchData.WeatherForecast, BlazorApp3, Version=1.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=null]].GetEnumerator()
   at System.Linq.EnumerableQuery`1[[BlazorApp3.Pages.FetchData.WeatherForecast, BlazorApp3, Version=1.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=null]].System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable<T>.GetEnumerator()
   at System.Collections.Generic.LargeArrayBuilder`1[[BlazorApp3.Pages.FetchData.WeatherForecast, BlazorApp3, Version=1.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=null]].AddRange(IEnumerable`1 items)
   at System.Collections.Generic.EnumerableHelpers.ToArray[WeatherForecast](IEnumerable`1 source)
   at System.Linq.Enumerable.ToArray[WeatherForecast](IEnumerable`1 source)
   at BlazorApp3.Pages.FetchData.OnInitializedAsync()
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.ComponentBase.RunInitAndSetParametersAsync()
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.RenderTree.Renderer.GetErrorHandledTask(Task taskToHandle)
```

Working on a fix.

The issue here is that when you use methods on `System.Linq.Queryable` against an in-memory collection, they get re-written to the corresponding method on `System.Linq.Enumerable`. However, the linker doesn't know about this connection between the two types, since the connection is made using Reflection here:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/9c472545df220d7ae26329e1649f880c4ee127e8/src/libraries/System.Linq.Queryable/src/System/Linq/EnumerableRewriter.cs#L39-L45

There's 2 options I can see that will fix this.

1. We can annotate the above `FindEnumerableMethod` method with a `DynamicallyAccessedMembers` attribute, telling it to preserve methods on `System.Linq.Enumerable`.
    - The issue there is ALL the methods on `System.Linq.Enumerable` will be preserved as soon as you use a single method on `Queryable`. On my machine, that will add roughly 100 KB of uncompressed IL to a Blazor app.
2. We can annotate each individual `Queryable` method with a `DynamicDependency` attribute to the corresponding `Enumerable` method. That means only the `Enumerable` methods that are being used though `Queryable` will be preserved.
    - There is a bit of a maintenance issue here - we need to remember to add this attribute to any new `Queryable` method, but we can cover that with a unit test.

My plan is to take approach (2) to fix this.

> My plan is to take approach (2) to fix this.

That sounds like the right one.

For the future, have we explored the idea of allowing the linker to execute code in an assembly?  I'm imagining if this scenario could instead be solved in the future with a variation on (1):
```C#
[DynamicallyAccessedMembersCallback(nameof(GetCorrespondingEnumerableMethod))]
public static class Queryable
{
    ...

    private static MemberInfo GetCorrespondingEnumerableMethod(MemberInfo source) =>
        typeof(Enumerable).GetMethod(source.Name); // something more complicated, but you get the idea
}
```
Just spitballing.  Even if we could make such a mechanism work, it could end up being way more complicated than its worth.

> but we can cover that with a unit test

FWIW, we already have similar unit tests about correspondance between Queryable and Enumerable:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/e87d2470773e48991b8e1d965d49b3ef03b303fe/src/libraries/System.Linq.Queryable/tests/Queryable.cs#L102-L112

review_comments: I didn't think it was necessary since the next line would NRE if it was null. Do we typically add `Assert.NonNull`s even if we dereference the variable?

We're inconsistent. Personally I prefer it in a case like this as not finding the delegate will make it null, the main condition we care about here, and asserting it rather than null ref'ing is likely to make it more diagnosable.
Does this end up keeping all the Sum overloads?  Is there a way to specify it should only keep the one for double?

Yes, it will keep all the Sum overloads. It is possible to fully specify the exact method, but it really complicates the signature. And in my opinion, makes this a lot more risky. We do get linker warnings if the method can't be resolved. But if we get the wrong one, we could have a bug.

For example:

```C#
[DynamicDependency("Where`1", typeof(Enumerable))]
```

would now become:

```C#
[DynamicDependency("Where`1(System.Collections.Generic.IEnumerable{``0},System.Func{``0,System.Boolean})", typeof(Enumerable))]
```

Do you think I should go ahead and change all of them to specify the exact signature?

Here's the start of what that would look like:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/commit/af0cfbd15294b90a28e2bc550c55ecd56ddbba1a
If it's risky then it's probably not worth it for this release. Maybe worth revisiting for the next.

It does seem more error-prone, but if the signatures would match up such that the unit test you have would find mismatches, then it would be a nice touch. Are there any where the signatures don't match?

But "not worth it for this release" sounds good to me.

`Sum` and `Average` are definitely the extreme cases here - there are 10 overloads of each (20 total, but we specify the generic type count in the signature, so the ILLinker will only preserve 10).

For Sum, doing it the way I proposed adds 2.5 KB of IL if you only use a single overload.
For Average, doing it the way I proposed adds 7 KB of IL if you only use a single overload.

> Are there any where the signatures don't match?

Basically all the signatures don't match exactly. `IQueryable` => `IEnumerable`, and `Expression<Func<...>>` => `Func<...>`. So we would need to encode that in the unit test as well.

Can you point me to where this reflection happens? I assume we need to suppress linker warnings in that spot because DynamicDependency only keeps stuff but doesn't help linker to analyze anything (as opposed to DynamicallyAccessedMembers annotations that both keep stuff and help analysis).

I wonder whether we can just write the reflection in a way that linker can analyze instead.

From a cursory look at reflection use around here, there are some ridiculously bad patterns. (E.g. constructing a delegate to something and grabbing a method info of the delegate, instead of simply doing a `typeof(X).GetMethod()` that is both fast and easy to analyze, etc.).

If this is about the pattern in EnumerableRewriter.VisitMethodCall, I'm not convinced that it can be made linker safe in general (and once we place a suppression on it, we'll get a warm and fuzzy feeling that it's safe).

This part is probably covered:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/6072e4d3a7a2a1493f514cdf4be75a3d56580e84/src/libraries/System.Linq.Queryable/src/System/Linq/EnumerableRewriter.cs#L39-L45

But this part looks pretty suspicious to me:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/6072e4d3a7a2a1493f514cdf4be75a3d56580e84/src/libraries/System.Linq.Queryable/src/System/Linq/EnumerableRewriter.cs#L48-L51

Are we convinced this part is also okay? Because if not, another solution is just to mark Queryable as not linker safe.

@MichalStrehovsky I think in the reported issue the reflection call is at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/6072e4d3a7a2a1493f514cdf4be75a3d56580e84/src/libraries/System.Linq.Queryable/src/System/Linq/EnumerableRewriter.cs#L218 but it's possible there are more code paths using reflection in queryable implementation

@MichalStrehovsky I discussed this with Eric and you're right the second part with `FindMethod` is not solved and honestly that one is basically impossible to solve fully - I can see us doing something which would solve it for this specific case, but the way the API is designed we probably can't ever get the right information into the right place (linker would basically have to understand expression tree nodes and be able to track some additional metadata about them).

My understanding is that this change is meant as a fix for an issue reported in 5.0 - regression compared to Blazor 3.2. It's not meant as a full solution to the Linq problem.

> My understanding is that this change is meant as a fix for an issue reported in 5.0 - regression compared to Blazor 3.2. It's not meant as a full solution to the Linq problem.

Correct.

If you want to see the current linker warnings on this library, check out the suppressions file being added in @layomia's PR #40691:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/751582618e20d512eb5d4ce09877bae24c094b58/src/libraries/System.Linq.Queryable/src/ILLink/ILLink.Suppressions.xml

There's 110 of them - so lots of work here to make the full library trim-safe.

> the second part with FindMethod is not solved and honestly that one is basically impossible to solve fully

The more I look at it, the more I think this kind of code could never truly be trim-safe. My understanding of that `FindMethod` case is that if you have 2 methods:

```C#

public static void Foo<T>(Expression<Func<T>> func);
public static void Foo<T>(Func<T> func);

```

And the current `Expression` is pointing at the first method, `FindMethod` will find the second method (since `Expression<>` gets [stripped during the rewrite](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/9c472545df220d7ae26329e1649f880c4ee127e8/src/libraries/System.Linq.Queryable/src/System/Linq/EnumerableRewriter.cs#L289-L302). How could we ever model this in the ILLinker?

And the problem gets worse as we expand to user code, because anyone could write an `ExpressionVisitor` which could do any sort of reflection policy.

It's hard to make 20 year of legacy APIs trimming friendly.

I think we'll end up with a type-level trimming mode eventually (where entire types are kept and linker warnings are scaled back to what's unsafe when trimming whole types only) - it will not be as efficient at deleting stuff as member level trimming, but patterns like this would be safe in it.

It might well be that Queryable will only be safe in this more conservative trimming mode and will warn otherwise. Of course this code should be investigated - is the pattern match documented and are people relying on it, or is this for internal use somewhere etc.?
